title: Subsets
description:
Given an integer array `nums` of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set).

The solution set must not contain duplicate subsets. You may return the subsets in any order, and the elements within each subset may also be in any order.
constraints: All the numbers of nums are unique.
hints: Each element in nums has two independent choices: either include it in the current subset or exclude it.
Use backtracking with a start index so every subset is generated in increasing index order, preventing duplicate subsets.
Alternatively, iterate over all integers from 0 to 2^n - 1 and interpret each bitmask as a subset selection.

examples.explanation: A single-element array [0] has 2^1 = 2 subsets: [] and [0].

title: Subsets II
description:
Given an integer array `nums` that may contain duplicates, return all possible subsets (the power set).

The solution set must not contain duplicate subsets. Two subsets are considered identical if they contain the same elements with the same multiplicities. You may return the subsets in any order, and the elements within each subset may also be in any order.
hints: Sort the input array first so identical elements become adjacent.
During backtracking at recursion level starting at `start`, if `i > start` and `nums[i] == nums[i - 1]`, skip `nums[i]` to avoid generating duplicate subsets at the same depth.
Notice that skipping only when `i > start` still allows using duplicate values in deeper recursion levels (e.g., [2, 2]).

examples.explanation: The unique subsets of [1, 2, 2] are [], [1], [2], [1, 2], [2, 2], and [1, 2, 2]. Duplicate [1, 2] and [2] are excluded.
The single-element array [0] has 2 unique subsets: [] and [0].
Sorting gives [1, 4, 4, 4, 4]; every subset picks 0 or 1 copy of 1 and between 0 and 4 copies of 4, yielding 2 * 5 = 10 unique subsets.

title: Permutations
description:
Given an array `nums` of distinct integers, return all possible permutations of its elements.

Each permutation must contain every element of `nums` exactly once in a specific order. You may return the list of permutations in any order.
constraints: All the integers of nums are unique.
hints: Build each permutation position by position using recursion, keeping track of which elements are already placed.
You can either maintain a boolean `used` array of length `n` or swap each remaining candidate into the current index `first` and swap back on return.

examples.explanation: There are 2! = 2 permutations of [0, 1]: [0, 1] and [1, 0].
A single-element array [1] has only 1! = 1 permutation: [1].

title: Permutations II
description:
Given a collection of numbers `nums` that might contain duplicates, return all possible unique permutations in any order.

Each permutation must have the same length and element multiplicities as `nums`, and no two returned permutations may be identical.
hints: Sort `nums` first so duplicate values sit next to each other.
Track used indices with a boolean array `used`. To ensure identical values are placed in a single canonical order, skip index `i` when `i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1] and not used[i - 1]`.
Alternatively, count frequencies of each unique value in a map and branch once per unique value with remaining count > 0.

examples.explanation: There are 3! / 2! = 3 unique permutations of [1, 1, 2]: [1, 1, 2], [1, 2, 1], and [2, 1, 1].
All elements are distinct, so all 3! = 6 permutations are returned.
There are 4! / (2! * 2!) = 6 unique permutations of [2, 2, 1, 1].

title: Combination Sum
description:
Given an array of distinct positive integers `candidates` and a target integer `target`, return a list of all unique combinations of `candidates` where the chosen numbers sum to `target`.

The same number may be chosen from `candidates` an unlimited number of times. Two combinations are unique if the frequency of at least one of the chosen numbers is different. You may return the combinations in any order, and the numbers inside each combination may be in any order.
constraints: All elements of candidates are distinct.
The number of unique combinations summing to target is less than 150 for every test case.
hints: Sort `candidates` so you can stop exploring a branch as soon as the current candidate exceeds the remaining target.
Pass a `start` index into your recursive helper so combinations are built in non-decreasing index order and permutations of the same multiset are never repeated.
Because each candidate may be reused, pass `i` (not `i + 1`) as the next `start` index when recursing after picking `candidates[i]`.

examples.explanation: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 and 7 = 7 are the only two unique combinations summing to 7.
The unique combinations summing to 8 are [2, 2, 2, 2], [2, 3, 3], and [3, 5].
Since every candidate is at least 2, no combination can sum to 1, so return [].

title: Combination Sum II
description:
Given a collection of candidate numbers `candidates` (which may contain duplicates) and a target number `target`, find all unique combinations in `candidates` where the candidate numbers sum to `target`.

Each element in `candidates` may be used at most once in a combination. The solution set must not contain duplicate combinations. You may return the combinations in any order, and the numbers within each combination may be in any order.
hints: Sort `candidates` so duplicates are adjacent and values exceeding the remaining target allow immediate pruning.
Pass `i + 1` to the recursive call so each array element is used at most once.
Skip duplicate choices at the same recursion depth with `if i > start and candidates[i] == candidates[i - 1]: continue`.

examples.explanation: Using each element at most once, the unique combinations summing to 8 are [1, 1, 6], [1, 2, 5], [1, 7], and [2, 6].
The unique combinations summing to 5 are [1, 2, 2] and [5].
Every candidate is greater than 2, so no combination sums to 2.

title: Combination Sum III
description:
Find all valid combinations of `k` distinct numbers that sum up to `n` such that the following conditions are true:

- Only numbers `1` through `9` are used.
- Each number is used at most once.

Return a list of all possible valid combinations. The list must not contain the same combination twice, and the combinations (as well as elements inside each combination) may be returned in any order.
hints: Pick digits in strictly increasing order from 1 to 9 so every digit is used at most once and combinations are automatically unique.
Prune branches early: if `need` digits remain to be chosen starting at `start`, stop when `9 - start + 1 < need` or when the smallest possible sum exceeds the remaining target.

examples.explanation: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 is the only combination of 3 distinct digits from 1..9 summing to 7.
The three valid combinations of 3 distinct digits summing to 9 are [1, 2, 6], [1, 3, 5], and [2, 3, 4].
The smallest possible sum of 4 distinct digits from 1..9 is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, so no combination sums to 1.

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
description:
Given a string `digits` containing digits from `'2'` to `'9'` inclusive, return all possible letter combinations that the number could represent on a standard telephone keypad:

- `'2'` -> `"abc"`, `'3'` -> `"def"`, `'4'` -> `"ghi"`, `'5'` -> `"jkl"`
- `'6'` -> `"mno"`, `'7'` -> `"pqrs"`, `'8'` -> `"tuv"`, `'9'` -> `"wxyz"`

If `digits` is empty, return an empty list `[]`. You may return the combinations in any order.
constraints: digits[i] is a digit in the range ['2', '9'].
hints: Handle the empty input `""` explicitly by returning `[]` rather than `[""]`.
Use backtracking indexed by position `idx` in `digits`: for each letter mapped to `digits[idx]`, append it, recurse to `idx + 1`, and backtrack.

examples.explanation: Digit '2' maps to a/b/c and '3' maps to d/e/f, producing 3 * 3 = 9 combinations.
An empty digit string produces no letter combinations, so return [].
Digit '2' maps to the three single-letter strings "a", "b", and "c".

solutionCode.python:
class Solution:
    def letterCombinations(self, digits: str) -> List[str]:
        if not digits:
            return []
        keypad = {
            "2": "abc",
            "3": "def",
            "4": "ghi",
            "5": "jkl",
            "6": "mno",
            "7": "pqrs",
            "8": "tuv",
            "9": "wxyz",
        }
        res: List[str] = []
        path: List[str] = []
        n = len(digits)

        def dfs(idx: int) -> None:
            if idx == n:
                res.append("".join(path))
                return
            for ch in keypad[digits[idx]]:
                path.append(ch)
                dfs(idx + 1)
                path.pop()

        dfs(0)
        return res

title: Generate Parentheses
description:
Given `n` pairs of parentheses, write a function to generate all combinations of well-formed (balanced) parentheses strings of length `2 * n`.

A string of `'('` and `')'` is well-formed if every opening parenthesis `'('` has a matching closing parenthesis `')'` and no prefix of the string contains more `')'` characters than `'('` characters. For `n = 0`, return `[""]` (a list containing a single empty string). You may return the valid strings in any order.
hints: Build each string one character at a time while tracking how many '(' and ')' have been placed so far.
You can place '(' whenever openCount < n, and you can place ')' only when closeCount < openCount.
Pruning invalid prefixes early guarantees every leaf reached at length 2 * n is a valid combination, avoiding wasted work.

examples.explanation: There are 5 distinct well-formed combinations using 3 pairs of parentheses (the 3rd Catalan number, C_3 = 5).
With 1 pair of parentheses, the only valid combination is "()".

title: N-Queens
description:
The n-queens puzzle is the problem of placing `n` queens on an `n x n` chessboard such that no two queens attack each other. Two queens attack each other if they share the same row, column, or diagonal.

Given an integer `n`, return all distinct solutions to the n-queens puzzle. You may return the solutions in any order. Each solution is represented as a list of `n` strings of length `n` ordered from row `0` to row `n - 1`, where `'Q'` indicates a queen and `'.'` indicates an empty square. If no valid placement exists, return an empty list `[]`.
hints: Because each row must contain exactly one queen, place queens one row at a time from row 0 to row n - 1.
Track occupied columns, main diagonals (row - col), and anti-diagonals (row + col) in O(1) using sets, boolean arrays, or bitmasks.
Bitmasks allow computing all safe columns for the current row in a single bitwise expression and iterating only over valid set bits.

examples.explanation: For n = 4, there are exactly 2 distinct valid board configurations where no two queens share a row, column, or diagonal.
For n = 1, a single queen placed at (0, 0) forms the unique solution [["Q"]].

solutionCode.python:
class Solution:
    def solveNQueens(self, n: int) -> List[List[str]]:
        res: List[List[str]] = []
        queens = [-1] * n
        full = (1 << n) - 1
        row_strs = ["." * c + "Q" + "." * (n - 1 - c) for c in range(n)]

        def backtrack(row: int, cols: int, d1: int, d2: int) -> None:
            if row == n:
                res.append([row_strs[c] for c in queens])
                return
            avail = full & ~(cols | d1 | d2)
            while avail:
                bit = avail & -avail
                avail ^= bit
                col = bit.bit_length() - 1
                queens[row] = col
                backtrack(row + 1, cols | bit, (d1 | bit) << 1, (d2 | bit) >> 1)

        backtrack(0, 0, 0, 0)
        return res

title: Sudoku Solver
description:
Write a program to solve a `9 x 9` Sudoku puzzle by filling the empty cells in-place.

A Sudoku solution must satisfy all of the following rules:
1. Each of the digits `'1'-'9'` must occur exactly once in each row.
2. Each of the digits `'1'-'9'` must occur exactly once in each column.
3. Each of the digits `'1'-'9'` must occur exactly once in each of the nine `3 x 3` sub-boxes of the grid.

The `'.'` character indicates an empty cell. Modify `board` in-place so that it contains the unique valid solution; do not return anything.
constraints: It is guaranteed that the input board has a single unique solution.
hints: Maintain three 9-element bitmask arrays (for rows, columns, and 3x3 boxes) to check valid candidate digits for cell (r, c) in O(1) time.
The 3x3 box index for cell (r, c) is (r // 3) * 3 + (c // 3).
To solve hard Sudokus rapidly, apply the Minimum Remaining Values (MRV) heuristic: always branch next on the empty cell with the fewest legal candidates.

examples.explanation: Each empty '.' cell is filled in-place so every row, column, and 3x3 sub-box contains the digits '1' through '9' exactly once.
Even with an entirely blank middle row, constraint propagation and backtracking determine the unique valid completion.

solutionCode.python:
class Solution:
    def solveSudoku(self, board: List[List[str]]) -> None:
        rows = [0] * 9
        cols = [0] * 9
        boxes = [0] * 9
        empties: List[tuple[int, int]] = []

        for r in range(9):
            for c in range(9):
                ch = board[r][c]
                if ch == ".":
                    empties.append((r, c))
                else:
                    bit = 1 << (ord(ch) - ord("1"))
                    rows[r] |= bit
                    cols[c] |= bit
                    boxes[(r // 3) * 3 + (c // 3)] |= bit

        n = len(empties)

        def dfs(idx: int) -> bool:
            if idx == n:
                return True
            best = idx
            best_cnt = 10
            best_mask = 0
            for i in range(idx, n):
                r, c = empties[i]
                bi = (r // 3) * 3 + (c // 3)
                avail = 0x1FF & ~(rows[r] | cols[c] | boxes[bi])
                cnt = avail.bit_count()
                if cnt == 0:
                    return False
                if cnt < best_cnt:
                    best_cnt = cnt
                    best = i
                    best_mask = avail
                    if cnt == 1:
                        break

            empties[idx], empties[best] = empties[best], empties[idx]
            r, c = empties[idx]
            bi = (r // 3) * 3 + (c // 3)
            m = best_mask
            while m:
                bit = m & -m
                m ^= bit
                digit = bit.bit_length()
                board[r][c] = chr(ord("0") + digit)
                rows[r] |= bit
                cols[c] |= bit
                boxes[bi] |= bit
                if dfs(idx + 1):
                    return True
                rows[r] ^= bit
                cols[c] ^= bit
                boxes[bi] ^= bit
                board[r][c] = "."
            empties[idx], empties[best] = empties[best], empties[idx]
            return False

        dfs(0)

title: Word Search
description:
Given an `m x n` grid of characters `board` and a string `word`, return `true` if `word` exists in the grid, and `false` otherwise.

The word can be constructed from letters of sequentially adjacent cells, where adjacent cells are horizontally or vertically neighboring (diagonal moves are not allowed). The same cell may not be used more than once in forming the word. Character matching is case-sensitive.
constraints: board and word consist only of lowercase and uppercase English letters.
hints: Start a depth-first search from every cell matching word[0], exploring up, down, left, and right neighbors.
Mark the current cell as visited (for example, temporarily overwriting it in-place with a sentinel like '#') before recursing, and restore its original character when backtracking.
Prune impossible searches early: verify the board has enough occurrences of every character in word, and consider reversing word when its last character is rarer on the board than its first.

examples.explanation: The path (0,0)->(0,1)->(0,2)->(1,2)->(2,2)->(2,1) spells "ABCCED" without reusing any cell.
The path (1,3)->(2,3)->(2,2) spells "SEE".
"ABCB" cannot be formed because moving back from 'C' to 'B' would reuse cell (0,1).

title: Palindrome Partitioning
description:
Given a string `s`, partition `s` such that every substring of the partition is a palindrome. Return all possible palindrome partitionings of `s`.

You may return the list of partitionings in any order, but within each partitioning the substrings must appear in left-to-right order so that concatenating them reproduces `s`.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.
hints: Use backtracking starting at index 0: try every prefix s[start..end] that is a palindrome, append it to the current path, and recurse from end + 1.
Precompute an n x n boolean DP table isPal[i][j] indicating whether s[i..j] is a palindrome so each palindrome check during backtracking takes O(1) time.
A substring s[i..j] is a palindrome if s[i] == s[j] and either j - i <= 2 or isPal[i + 1][j - 1] is true.

examples.explanation: "aab" can be partitioned into ["a","a","b"] or ["aa","b"].
A single character is always a palindrome, giving [["a"]].
"aba" can be split into three single-character palindromes or kept whole as ["aba"].

title: Restore IP Addresses
description:
A valid IPv4 address consists of exactly four integers separated by single dots `'.'`. Each integer must be between `0` and `255` (inclusive) and cannot have leading zeros (for example, `"0.1.2.201"` and `"192.168.1.1"` are valid, whereas `"0.011.255.245"` and `"192.168.1.312"` are invalid).

Given a string `s` containing only digits, return all possible valid IPv4 addresses that can be formed by inserting three dots into `s`. You cannot reorder or remove any digits in `s`. You may return the valid IP addresses in any order.
hints: An IPv4 address has 4 segments, each 1 to 3 digits long, so strings shorter than 4 or longer than 12 characters can never form a valid IP.
Backtrack by placing 4 segments one at a time, pruning whenever the remaining digits cannot fit in the remaining segments (remaining < partsLeft or remaining > 3 * partsLeft).
A segment of length > 1 is invalid if it starts with '0', and a 3-digit segment is invalid if its numeric value exceeds 255.

examples.explanation: The two valid ways to insert three dots into "25525511135" are "255.255.11.135" and "255.255.111.35".
Each single '0' forms one valid octet, producing "0.0.0.0".
All five splits respect the 0..255 range and forbid multi-digit octets with leading zeros.

title: Word Break II
description:
Given a string `s` and a dictionary of strings `wordDict`, add spaces in `s` to construct a sentence where each word is a valid dictionary word. Return all such possible sentences in any order.

Note that the same word in the dictionary may be reused multiple times in the segmentation. If no valid segmentation exists, return an empty list `[]`.
constraints: s and wordDict[i] consist of only lowercase English letters.
All the strings of wordDict are unique.
The input is generated such that the number of valid sentences does not exceed 10^4.
hints: Store wordDict in a hash set and track the maximum word length so each prefix lookup at index i checks at most maxLen substrings.
Plain backtracking can repeatedly explore dead-end suffixes (such as "aaaa...ab" with words "a", "aa", ...). Memoize the list of valid sentences starting from each index i.
For a suffix s[i:], whenever s[i:j] is in the dictionary, combine s[i:j] with every memoized sentence returned for index j.

examples.explanation: "catsanddog" can be segmented as "cats and dog" or "cat sand dog".

examples.output: ["pine apple pen apple","pine applepen apple","pineapple pen apple"]
examples.explanation: Words like "apple" may be reused, yielding three distinct valid sentences.
No sequence of dictionary words covers "catsandog" completely, so return [].

title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
description:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return `true` if it is possible to divide this array into `k` non-empty subsets whose sums are all equal, and `false` otherwise.

Every element of `nums` must be assigned to exactly one of the `k` subsets.
hints: First check quick necessary conditions: the total sum must be divisible by k, and the largest element cannot exceed target = sum(nums) / k.

Sort nums in descending order so larger elements fail early, and fill one bucket to target at a time. When starting a new empty bucket, force the first unused element into it to eliminate k! permutations of identical buckets.
Because n <= 16, represent the set of used elements as a bitmask and memoize failed bitmasks (the current bucket's partial sum is uniquely determined by the bitmask as usedSum % target).

examples.explanation: The array sums to 20 and can be partitioned into 4 subsets of sum 5: (5), (1, 4), (2, 3), and (2, 3).
The total sum is 10, which is not divisible by k = 3, so no equal-sum partition exists.
Although 2+2+2+2+3+4+5 = 20 is divisible by 4 (target 5), the four 2s cannot all be combined into subsets of sum 5 with the remaining elements.
